title: What to wish for
translation: Well, once you're born into this world, there's plenty to wish for.

The emperor is too far above us to even talk about. Even his most distant relatives aren't ordinary humans, and that makes them special. The regent, obviously. But even an ordinary noble looks impressive once the court gives him his own guards, and his children and grandchildren keep a certain grace even after the family has come down in the world. Below that, people climb as high as their rank allows, have their moment, and look very pleased with themselves. They think they're doing great. It's actually rather sad.

Nobody envies a priest. Sei Shōnagon said people treat them like a lump of wood, and she wasn't wrong. And the ones who throw their weight around and make a big fuss? Not impressive. The old hermit Zōga supposedly said that chasing fame just makes you miserable, and it's probably not what the Buddha had in mind. Someone who has actually walked away from it all is another matter, though. There's something to be said for that.

Looks and manners matter. If someone talks pleasantly, has some charm and doesn't go on too long, you could sit with them for hours. It's a shame when someone you admired turns out to be disappointing underneath. You're born with your looks and your class, but your mind? Why shouldn't it get wiser and wiser if you work on it? Take someone good-looking and decent, but with no education: they slip down a level, end up among plain, ordinary people, and get beaten by them hands down. What a waste.

Ideally, you'd know the classics properly, and when people write poems or play music, you'd be able to join in. You'd know court etiquette so well that people watch you to see how it's done. That would be something. It helps if your handwriting still looks good when you're just dashing something off, and if you can sing and keep the beat when there's music. And when someone offers you a drink, say no at first. But only at first. A man should be able to hold his liquor.

literal: Well now, being born into this world, the things one should wish for seem to be many.
The emperor's rank is very awe-inspiring.
Down to the last leaves of the bamboo garden, not being of human seed is noble.
The state of the first man (the regent) goes without saying; even an ordinary person, at the level of being granted guards and the like, looks splendid.
His children and grandchildren, even if they have declined, are still graceful.
Those further below, each according to their station, meet with good times and look pleased with themselves; they themselves probably think they are splendid, but it is very regrettable.
There is surely nothing as unenviable as a priest: that Sei Shōnagon wrote 'They are thought of by people like a piece of wood' is indeed so.
Though they make a great noise with their power, they do not look splendid.
As the holy man Zōga is said to have said, it is painful with (the pursuit of) fame, and I feel it probably goes against the Buddha's teaching.
A thorough world-renouncer, on the contrary, may well have something desirable about him.
In people, it is surely desirable that their looks and bearing be excellent.
When they speak, not unpleasant to hear, with charm, and not many words: that is what one would like to face without tiring.
That a person one thought splendid should show a true nature that makes one think less of them: that would be regrettable.
Rank and looks may be what one is born with, but the mind: why, if one moves it from wise to wiser, would it not move?
Even a person good in looks and disposition, if without learning, falls in standing, mixes even with people of unpleasant faces, and is overwhelmed without contest: that is a disappointing thing.

What one would like to have: true learning in letters, composing Chinese poems, Japanese poetry, the way of music, and also knowledge of court precedent and public ceremonies, so as to be a model for others: that would be splendid.
Handwriting not clumsy, writing in a running hand, a voice pleasant and keeping the rhythm, declining politely, yet not being a non-drinker: that is what is good in a man.

notes.text: 'Well now', 'well then'. The 1925 edition notes that this sentence reads as a direct continuation of the preface: he sat down to write whatever comes to mind, and this is what came first.
'The bamboo garden': a poetic name for the imperial family, from a Chinese story about a prince's bamboo garden. The 1925 edition glosses it simply as 'the imperial family'.
'The first man': the regent (摂政 or 関白), the most powerful person at court after the emperor.

notes.quote: 舎人などたまはる際は
notes.text: {舎人|とねり}: guards or attendants that the court granted to high nobles as an honour. Having an official escort was a visible sign of rank.

notes.quote: 人には木の端のやうに思はるるよ
notes.text: A quotation from Sei Shōnagon's Pillow Book, from a passage about parents who make their son a priest: people treat a priest 'like a piece of wood', as if he had no feelings. Kenkō read her closely and quotes her more than once.
Zōga (917–1003), a monk famous for strange behaviour that he used to escape honours and fame. {名聞|みやうもん}ぐるしく: '{名聞|みやうもん} (fame) is painful'.

notes.quote: 人品容貌こそ生れつきたらめ、心はなどか
notes.text: こそ … め, followed by a comma: when a こそ clause does not end the sentence, it means 'although'. 'Looks and rank may be inborn, but the mind…?' などか … む is a rhetorical question: 'why would it not…? (It would.)'
{才|ざえ}: learning, especially Chinese learning. Not modern {才|さい} 'talent'.
A false friend: {作文|さくもん} is composing Chinese poetry, the most prestigious skill at court. Modern {作文|さくぶん} is a school essay.
{拍子|ひやうし}: rhythm, keeping time. The 1925 edition gives the reading はうし, which this page keeps; the usual historical spelling is ひやうし (modern ひょうし).

notes.quote: 下戸ならぬこそ男はよけれ
notes.text: {下戸|げこ}: someone who cannot drink alcohol. The word is still used today. After a long, serious list of ideal skills, the section ends on a light, practical point: he should refuse a drink politely at first, but be able to drink.
